While everyone has their own tastes and their subjective take on whether a movie is "good" or "bad" is always valid, there are objective ways to measure the quality of a movie: whether it communicates its message effectively, whether it has elements that don't accomplish what they're supposed to or take the audience out of the moment or are simply distracting, whether the story flows properly and explains everything that needs explaining, etc. When using this more objective definition, I prefer the term "failed" movies, because that's what they are: movies that failed to communicate what they set out to communicate for whatever reasons.

With that in mind, there are lots of reasons to enjoy failed art. The most obvious is that they're often accidentally funny in their failure, because comedy that wasn't intended to be comedy is still entertaining to watch and because there's something satisfying about an artist swinging for the fences as hard as they can and coming nowhere near close to hitting the ball. There's also a lot of value in failed movies for people who understand and appreciate the mechanics of film as a medium and can benefit from seeing what happens when things are done incorrectly and asking what could be improved. Failed movies also tend to be daring, failing because they decided to try something really new and challenging instead of making a safe, derivative movie and it just didn't come together like they'd hoped, and those movies often have kernels of really interesting ideas that you just wouldn't find in any other movie and that you can see how they might have been great if certain decisions were made differently. And of course there is the appeal of kitsch, of liking something regardless of its "objective" quality just because you like it and you enjoy liking it and sharing that enjoyment with others who like it.

I guess the TL;DR is that failed movies often (I'd argue always) have *some* value as works of art, whether they're accidental comedy or a cautionary tale or an exploration of how the mechanics of film fail sometimes. I think that we should all strive to ask ourselves, when we see a film that is "bad", exactly why it is bad and maybe even why parts of it are good or enjoyable despite that. I know ever since I decided to do that, I've started liking all movies a lot more.
